programme: A stress-induced, cell-death-coupled inflammatory transcription module built from ATF3, BRD4, KLF6 and BCL3: BRD4 (BET bromodomain reader) controls ATF3 through an H3K27ac–ATF3 chromatin axis, ATF3 represses SLC7A11 to drive ferroptosis and sits upstream of ATF4/DDIT3-type integrated-stress-response targets, KLF6 independently drives ferroptosis via an NSUN2/NCOA4 route, and BCL3 (an atypical IκB) sits on the NF-κB arm (RELA, NFKB1, TNF, IL6, IL10, CXCL8) that is co-activated with this stress response.
role_in_a: In Sjögren's, BRD4 has been identified directly as a pyroptosis-related biomarker/candidate target, and ATF3 is linked to corneal nerve degeneration and ocular pain in Sjögren's-associated dry eye — consistent with the same stress/programmed-cell-death axis operating in exocrine and ocular-surface tissue injury.
role_in_b: In stroke, all four carrying factors are repeatedly and independently documented driving ischemia-reperfusion injury: ATF3 and KLF6 each promote neuronal ferroptosis through distinct routes (SLC7A11 repression; NSUN2/NCOA4), BRD4 controls ATF3 and blood-brain-barrier integrity, and BCL3 appears in ischemic-stroke transcriptomic and neuroinflammation studies as part of the NF-κB response.
shared_axis: Both networks are built from blood, so the concordance most plausibly reflects a circulating stress/inflammatory transcriptional state common to acute ischemic injury and chronic autoimmune epithelitis, rather than identical tissue pathology; Sjögren's syndrome carries a recognized elevated cerebrovascular/stroke risk from chronic systemic inflammation and vasculopathy, giving a plausible route by which the same leukocyte stress-response programme would be active in both conditions.
reasoning: The module is clearly nameable and its stroke role is strongly documented across multiple independent papers for three of the four carrying factors (ATF3, KLF6, BCL3), with BRD4 mechanistically linking ATF3 through a cited chromatin axis. But only ATF3 and BRD4 have any Sjögren's-specific citation, each from a single paper, and the one paper spanning both diseases (39995125) is a general review rather than a direct link — so the disease-disease connection here rests on known Sjögren's-stroke comorbidity and reasoning about a shared circulating stress signature, not on anything retrieved that ties the two together directly.
support: PMID 40605044 — BRD4 controls ATF3 via H3K27ac to drive neuronal ferroptosis/inflammation in a stroke model, the one paper directly linking two carrying factors; PMID 41314556 — ATF3 represses SLC7A11 to drive ferroptosis in ischemic stroke; PMID 42630848 and 40044488 — ATF3 in mitochondrial homeostasis/ischemia-reperfusion in stroke; PMID 41478321 and 39710598 — KLF6 drives neuronal ferroptosis in OGD/R and MCAO stroke models; PMID 40715883 — BCL3 among core genes in ischemic stroke transcriptomics; PMID 41410587 — BRD4 as a pyroptosis-related biomarker gene in Sjögren's syndrome; PMID 39839966 — ATF3-linked corneal nerve degeneration/ocular pain in Sjögren's dry eye; PMID 39995125 — reviews ISR modulators across neurological disease, mentions both diseases but does not connect them mechanistically.
how_to_falsify: In Sjögren's patient-derived salivary/lacrimal gland epithelial cells or PBMCs under stress (e.g. IFN or hypoxic challenge), knock down BRD4 and measure ATF3 and downstream ferroptosis markers (SLC7A11, NCOA4/KLF6 targets) alongside NF-κB output (BCL3, TNF, IL6); if BRD4 loss fails to suppress ATF3 and this ferroptosis/NF-κB signature in Sjögren's cells the way it does in ischemic neuronal (OGD/R) models, the claim that the two diseases share this specific module is wrong.
caveats: Tissue pairing is blood|blood — the networks are built from circulating cells, but nearly all of the cited literature evidence for these factors comes from CNS/neuronal tissue (MCAO, OGD/R models) or glandular/ocular-surface tissue, not blood, so the retrieved mechanisms are extrapolated onto a blood-derived signature rather than confirmed there. Only 21 patient-group comparisons from 4 independent cohort pairs support this, a modest base. Sjögren's-side evidence is thin: only 2 of the 12 concordant factors (ATF3, BRD4) have any disease-specific citation, each a single paper, and the remaining factors (FOXL1, TFEC, SP2, POU2F2, ELK4, ARID5A, TCF7L2, E2F4) returned nothing on-topic for this pair despite being concordant — they are not part of the named programme. The tissue-generic exclusion list removed several classic inflammatory/differentiation regulators (IRF1, FOXO3, FOXO4, RUNX2, SMAD3, LEF1, E2F1) that might otherwise be reached for as the 'obvious' immune explanation — their absence here is by design, not a gap. Single-view factors (MAML2, ZXDC, HLX, ZKSCAN7, HEYL, SIRT6) reflect one patient subgroup each and should not be read into this account.
